items.passage: Bergmann’s rule holds that individuals of a species tend to be smaller in warmer climates, since a smaller body dissipates heat more efficiently. For migratory birds, however, diminished body size also elevates the metabolic cost of flight—a considerable liability on journeys spanning thousands of kilometers—whereas proportionally longer wings reduce that cost. Analyzing 70,716 specimens of 52 migratory species that died after colliding with buildings in Chicago between 1978 and 2016, Brian Weeks and colleagues determined that tarsus length, a standard proxy for body size, decreased by 2.4% as summer temperatures on the species’ breeding grounds increased. Over the same period, wing length increased by 1.3%, a change that the researchers propose ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: may have helped the birds shed heat on their warming breeding grounds, adding to the cooling advantage that their smaller bodies already provided.
may have compensated for the 2.4% decrease in tarsus length, so that the birds’ overall body size changed little over the period studied.
may have helped the birds keep up their long migrations, which their smaller bodies had made more difficult by causing them to retain more heat in flight.
may have offset a cost that the birds’ response to warmer summers would otherwise have imposed on their long migrations.
items.explanation: Sentence 1 explains the shrinking: a smaller body sheds heat more efficiently, and the birds’ bodies shrank as summers on their breeding grounds warmed. The dash aside in sentence 2 names the price of that response: a smaller body raises the metabolic cost of flight, a liability on long migrations, while proportionally longer wings reduce that cost. Wings lengthened over the same period, so the researchers most plausibly see the longer wings as offsetting the flight cost that the warming-driven shrinking would otherwise have added. In choice D, “the birds’ response to warmer summers” is the shrinking and “a cost ... imposed on their long migrations” is the higher cost of flight.

A.recipe: right principle on the wrong variable (MIX)
A.why_wrong: The text links heat loss only to body size; the one effect it gives longer wings is a lower cost of flight, so nothing suggests the researchers see the wings as a way to shed heat.

B.recipe: right compensation on the wrong variable (MIX)
B.why_wrong: Tarsus length is “a standard proxy for body size,” so its decrease means the birds’ bodies shrank; the text gives longer wings one effect, a lower cost of flight, and nothing suggests they kept body size constant.

C.recipe: key content with the mechanism reversed in a subordinate clause (REV)
C.why_wrong: The first half fits the text, but the reason does not: sentence 1 says a smaller body dissipates heat more efficiently, so shrinking would not make the birds retain more heat; the difficulty the text names is the higher metabolic cost of flight.

band7_moves: S2 with two principles chained (Bergmann’s rule plus the flight-cost trade-off); the blank asks for the consequence that the second principle forces on the observed case
the decisive premise sits in a dash aside two sentences before the blank

key hedged as the evidence requires (“may have offset”) and stated one level up (“a cost that the birds’ response to warmer summers would otherwise have imposed”), so sentence 1, the dash aside and the wing change must be chained

distractors: MIX (the cooling role given to the wings), MIX (compensation aimed at body size instead of flight cost), REV hidden in a subordinate clause (the key’s claim in concrete words with Bergmann’s mechanism reversed); all three reuse true pieces of the text

sources.what: Weeks et al. 2020, Ecology Letters 23: 316-325: 70,716 individuals of 52 North American migratory species; warming summer temperatures predict body size reduction; wing length increased; hypothesis that longer wings are a compensatory adaptation to maintain migration as smaller bodies increased the metabolic cost of flight
Field Museum press release: birds that died hitting Chicago buildings, collected since 1978, data 1978-2016; tarsus decreased 2.4%, wing length increased 1.3%; Bergmann’s rule

items.subtype: Received view plus counterevidence (what the researchers contend)
items.passage: For more than half a century, laboratory experiments have demonstrated that an individual who witnesses an emergency is less likely to intervene when other witnesses are present than when alone. This phenomenon, the bystander effect, is frequently interpreted as evidence that victims in crowded public settings will rarely receive assistance. Yet when Richard Philpot and colleagues systematically coded surveillance footage of 219 actual conflicts in Amsterdam, Cape Town, and Lancaster, United Kingdom, they found that at least one bystander intervened in approximately nine of every ten conflicts and that the probability that someone intervened increased with the number of bystanders present. The researchers contend that their findings do not overturn the laboratory results but instead demonstrate that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a victim’s chances of being helped can rise with the number of bystanders even if each bystander, considered individually, becomes less inclined to intervene.
the reluctance to intervene seen in laboratories is produced by artificial settings and so does not arise among witnesses to actual conflicts.
a victim surrounded by many bystanders, though less likely to be helped than one with only a few witnesses, will still usually receive some help.
witnesses to real conflicts become more willing to intervene as more bystanders join them, which participants in laboratory experiments did not.
items.explanation: The laboratory finding concerns each individual witness, who is less likely to act when others are present. The footage records something else: whether anyone at all intervened, which happened in about nine of every ten conflicts and grew likelier as bystanders increased. Both hold at once if each person is somewhat less inclined to help but there are more people who might, which is how the researchers can keep the laboratory results while rejecting the fear that crowds leave victims unhelped. Choice A states that reconciliation. Because the footage measures only whether someone intervened, it cannot show that individual reluctance is absent in real settings or that each witness grows more willing.

B.recipe: level confusion presented as a limit on the laboratory results (MIX)
B.why_wrong: The footage records only whether at least one bystander intervened, so it cannot show that individual reluctance disappears outside the laboratory; a rising chance that someone helps is fully compatible with each witness being less inclined. Calling the laboratory effect an artifact also undercuts the results the researchers say they keep.

C.recipe: reversal hidden in the concession (REV), true tail
C.why_wrong: The tail fits the nine-in-ten rate, but the concession contradicts the footage: the more bystanders were present, the likelier someone intervened, so a victim with many bystanders was more likely, not less likely, to be helped.

D.recipe: swap of the level (MIX): aggregate read as individual
D.why_wrong: The footage shows how often someone intervened, not how willing each witness was; and saying real witnesses behave the opposite way from laboratory participants would overturn the laboratory results, which the researchers say their findings do not do.

band7_moves: S11 with the target of type T2: the blank reconstructs what the researchers contend, and the lead-in rules out any answer that overturns the received result
the new interpretation must account for all the evidence: the replicated individual-level effect, the 9-in-10 rate and the rise with group size
key is conditional (“even if”), hedged (“can rise”), and the shortest-but-one option

distractors: a level confusion that seems to honor “do not overturn” by confining the laboratory effect to laboratories (MIX), the received inference hidden in a concession beside the true nine-in-ten rate (REV), the aggregate read as individual willingness (MIX); all three are partly right

sources.what: Philpot, Liebst, Levine, Bernasco and Lindegaard 2020, American Psychologist 75(1): 66-75: CCTV of 219 public conflicts in the UK, the Netherlands and South Africa (Lancaster, Amsterdam, Cape Town); in 9 of 10 conflicts at least one bystander helped; more bystanders, greater likelihood that someone intervened; the study does not evaluate the individual-level bystander effect, and additional numbers may reduce individual helping propensity while providing a larger pool of helpers

PsyPost summary: traditional research measured an individual’s likelihood to intervene, not the aggregate likelihood that at least one person helps; each additional bystander increased the odds of help; the results challenge the popular view, not the experimental findings

items.passage: The tea plant cannot grow at the high elevations of western Tibet, and no documentary evidence of tea consumption in Tibet predates the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE). According to one tradition, tea was first introduced to Tibet as part of the dowry of the Chinese princess Wencheng, who married the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo in 641. Analyzing ancient botanical residues for caffeine, theanine, and phytoliths characteristic of tea, Houyuan Lu and colleagues identified tea among the funerary offerings of a Han emperor who died in 141 BCE, near present-day Xi’an, and among the remains at Gurgyam, a cemetery situated 4,290 meters above sea level in western Tibet and dated to the second or third century CE. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Wencheng’s dowry cannot have included any tea, since tea had already been carried into western Tibet centuries before her marriage to Songtsen Gampo.
tea had already been carried into western Tibet centuries before Wencheng’s marriage, so her dowry cannot have been what first brought tea to Tibet.
tea was present in Tibet centuries before Wencheng’s marriage, though only in places low enough for the tea plant to grow there.
tea had already been grown in western Tibet by the second or third century CE, long before Wencheng’s dowry could have introduced it there.
items.explanation: The rule in sentence 1 does the first step: tea cannot grow at the high elevations of western Tibet, so the tea at Gurgyam, 4,290 meters up in western Tibet, must have been brought there. The dates do the second: Gurgyam dates to the second or third century CE, centuries before Wencheng’s marriage in 641. So tea had been carried onto the plateau long before her dowry, which cannot have been what first brought tea to Tibet, as choice B says. That conclusion concerns only how tea first arrived: whatever the dowry may have contained, the findings say nothing about whether it included tea.

A.recipe: the key’s premise pushed to an invalid conclusion (EXT)
A.why_wrong: Its premise is the key’s, but the conclusion does not follow: tea’s earlier presence shows only that the dowry was not how tea first reached Tibet. Whatever the dowry may have contained, nothing in the findings bears on whether it included tea.

C.recipe: true first clause, then the growing rule misapplied to the tea itself (MIX)
C.why_wrong: Tea was in Tibet centuries before 641, but not only where the plant can grow: it was found at Gurgyam, 4,290 meters up in western Tibet, where the text says the plant cannot grow.

D.recipe: right date logic, carried swapped for grown (MIX)
D.why_wrong: The dates are right, but sentence 1 says the tea plant cannot grow at the high elevations of western Tibet, where Gurgyam lies, so the tea found there was brought in, not grown.

band7_moves: S3 with three dates or ranges (141 BCE, second or third century CE, Tang 618–907 overlapping the 641 marriage) and a rule stated in the first clause (tea cannot grow at western Tibet’s elevations, so its presence at Gurgyam means transport)
key is negative (“cannot have been what first brought tea to Tibet”) and needs the growing rule as well as the dates (“carried into western Tibet”)

distractors: a permutation set on the key’s own frame (grown in western Tibet; present only where the plant can grow), each keeping the true date logic, plus the key’s premise pushed to an invalid conclusion about the dowry’s contents (EXT); every option keeps a true detail
decisive rule sits in sentence 1, two sentences before the blank

sources.what: Lu et al. 2016, Scientific Reports 6: 18955: tea identified by caffeine, theanine and calcium phytoliths in the Han Yangling Mausoleum of the Jing Emperor Liu Qi (188–141 BCE) and at Gurgyam Cemetery, Ngari, 4290 m asl, dated second to third century CE; tea does not grow in Tibet; no records of tea entering Tibet before the Tang Dynasty (618–907 CE); claim that tea was introduced as part of Princess Wencheng’s dowry
Princess Wencheng married Songtsen Gampo in 641

items.passage: Modern strains of the bacterium responsible for tuberculosis in the Americas closely resemble European strains, implying that the disease was introduced by Europeans after 1492; skeletal evidence of pre-contact tuberculosis, however, contradicts that assumption. An alternative hypothesis holds that the disease accompanied the first human populations to reach the Americas, more than 15,000 years ago. Kirsten Bos and colleagues reconstructed three 1,000-year-old genomes of the pathogen from human skeletons in Peru and determined that they were most closely related not to any human-adapted strain but to strains that infect seals and sea lions; the team also dated the most recent common ancestor of all these strains, human-adapted ones included, to less than 6,000 years ago. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the disease reached Peru with the first people to arrive in the Americas and then spread from those people to the seals and sea lions along the coast.
the skeletal evidence of pre-contact tuberculosis was likely produced by some other disease, since the ancient Peruvian strains matched no human-adapted strain.
people in Peru likely acquired the disease from infected marine mammals rather than from the first people to reach the Americas or from Europeans.
the strains that caused tuberculosis in Peru 1,000 years ago are probably the ancestors of the strains that cause the disease in the Americas today.
items.explanation: The text names three possible sources. Europeans are ruled out because the Peruvian genomes are 1,000 years old, older than 1492. The first Americans are ruled out because the strains share an ancestor less than 6,000 years old, far later than people reached the Americas. The ancient strains are closest to those of seals and sea lions, so the remaining source is marine mammals, as choice C says. The ancient genomes are of the tuberculosis pathogen itself, recovered from human skeletons, so they confirm tuberculosis before 1492 rather than cast doubt on it.

A.why_wrong: The strains’ common ancestor lived less than 6,000 years ago, long after the first people reached the Americas more than 15,000 years ago, so the disease could not have come with them.

B.recipe: rescue of the received view by attacking the wrong premise (REV)
B.why_wrong: The ancient genomes are of “the pathogen” named in sentence 1, the tuberculosis bacterium, recovered from 1,000-year-old human skeletons, so people in Peru did have tuberculosis before 1492; that the strains resembled seal strains rather than human-adapted ones says where the disease came from, not that it was some other disease.

D.why_wrong: Modern American strains resemble European ones, whereas the ancient Peruvian strains were unlike any strain adapted to humans, so the ancient strains are not shown to be ancestors of today’s.

band7_moves: S4 elimination: three candidate sources, each met by a different kind of evidence (a date, a molecular age, a genetic resemblance)
permutation set: every option recombines the same pieces (first Americans, Europeans, seals, Peru, modern strains) with one link moved
key is an “other than” conclusion that rules out two routes at once, hedged (“likely”)
one premise (more than 15,000 years ago) sits two sentences before the blank, the other (less than 6,000 years) at the end of a 60-word sentence

sources.what: Bos et al. 2014, Nature 514: 494-497: modern American M. tuberculosis strains closely related to European ones, supporting post-contact introduction, which conflicts with archaeological evidence of pre-contact tuberculosis; three 1,000-year-old genomes from Peruvian skeletons, distinct from human-adapted forms and most closely related to strains adapted to seals and sea lions; most recent common ancestor of the complex less than 6,000 years ago
People reached the Americas at least 15,000 years ago

Full text (PMC): a Pleistocene dispersal following human movements could explain pre-contact presence (the first-humans hypothesis the text names); MRCA of the MTBC, which includes the human-adapted lineages, about 4,449 years before present; American strains most closely related to European ones
